answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: We support the improvement of methodology to quantify marginal emissions impact, and we believe it needs to be of equal viability and importance as the Scope 2 framework. Equal viable importance would therefore include methodology and a framework of recognition for consequential actions. Many institutions of higher education are limited in how many contractual instruments they can procure related to their deliverable load, and also limited in making investments in renewable electricity within their regions. These limitations include cost barriers and policy limitations, primarily. Because of these obstacles, some higher education institutions are making investments outside of their regions; targeting regions that rely more heavily on fossil generation allows these institutions to maintain their climate action leadership. Recognition for these actions is essential in ensuring these positive investments continue, especially in a federal policy environment that does not favor wind and solar in the short term. Providing a methodology for these investments to be recognized is also essential for ensuring a continuity in investment for less firm, yet more immediate renewable energy generation between now and 2035, as the Scope 2 Guidance evolves to clarify claims. To leave out consequential actions would only favor procurement of 24/7 carbon free electricity, which would disincentivize smaller entities and disproportionately create reliance on longer-range, firm strategies like geothermal, nuclear, and carbon capture and storage, leaving a gap in continuous positive climate impact, which only comes through the collective actions of a diversity of stakeholders. Current Scope 2 accounting does blur the line between claims associated with deliverable renewable energy at the time of its dispatchment, and consequential claims outside the entity’s deliverable load. While we are not clear on how the Protocol plans to recognize consequential actions, in theory we do support the concept of clear methods and recognition for both attributional claims and consequential claims.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: The general structure of the equation is an improvement from the equation in the GGEP in terms of hourly accuracy; however, neither of the equations presented allow for a full picture of consumption and procurement, so it is difficult to respond to this question with respect to all systems that might be considered in consequential impact assessments.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: Our answer might be yes, but not always. The pending methodology could ideally create guidance stipulating that biofuels projects and projects that have lesser weighted impact on the build margin are required to calculate secondary effects. Then, the methodology could stipulate that for other project scenarios, secondary effects are likely to be de minimis. If this is not possible, then we would change our answer to “no.”

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Reporting emissions impacts every year, or even every 5 years, is a more accurate accounting of the project’s actual impact against baseline. It is less possible to ensure that the baseline will remain static over the lifetime of a project, especially in rapidly changing energy grids. If, however, the calculation applied to determine the marginal emissions impact is more dynamic and holistic, it is possible that longer timeframes can be estimated. However, most organizations across sectors do not have many long-term electricity contracts, so annual reporting more accurately reflects the dynamic nature of electricity procurement for organizations of all sizes.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: Regulatory and timing tests should be required because projects are likely more common in regions that favor renewable energy with existing policy and investment. Truly additional domestic projects should be located in areas that are less permissive of these projects and have less historical precedent with respect to clean grid investment. However, these required tests should not be the only deciding factors in a project’s additionality. We marked the remaining tests as optional because we feel that project developers should have to demonstrate that their project passes at least 3 additionality tests; however, given a diversity of synchronous grid contexts, prescribing which 3 tests is not appropriate.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: We note that the feasibility of certain tests will depend on the grid region and data availability, so not all tests are feasible across all contexts. We also note that financial analyses can easily be gamed by inflating the cost of capital, so while feasible, financial analysis should always be paired with additional tests. Lastly, a positive list or performance standard could be a good parameter to build into the methodology by region, but it is not feasible applied across grid region contexts.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: Building upon our answer to question 21, in a particularly dirty grid region, it may be quite easy to pass a common practice test, a positive list or performance standard test, and a regulatory test. However in a cleaner grid region, a project may also be displacing fossil generation, but have a harder time passing these same tests, making a secondary option of passing a timing test, a barrier test, and a financial analysis test appropriate.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: The current GGEP uses a combination of methods to calculate OMER, which we support. It also makes sense to include more methodologies that could be combined depending on the data available and the contexts of the grid in which a project is connected. Further guidance could be included as to when certain tools might be used over others.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: A combination or weighted average of capacity additions, policy scenario, and capacity expansion modeling feel appropriate. While average grid emission rate is less reliable than what is used in even the current methodologies for estimated BMER, there may be scenarios in which average emission rate is appropriate, especially if combined with other methods, and, our members note that average emission rate may be the only data available in some areas to broadly calculate impacts.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Our members urge the protocol to keep the methodology simple and as accurate as possible so the intent is met and organizations can follow the standard, but making it too complicated or data intensive leaves many players (and, more importantly, climate action) behind in favor of a few large organizations with capacity and funds to chase GHG accounting details that do not substantially alter the outcomes.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Our focus is on a methodology that doesn’t constrict the definition of impact so much as to discourage the continuation of consequential projects or investment in those projects by voluntary actors. While ex-post data can show avoided emissions from projects at sub-hourly granularity and at the nodal level, there is wide variation in a project’s avoided emissions impact across temporal boundaries, and depending on its location.
